The “continental” Apennines

The start is at Ponte Organasco (457 m a.s.l.), and things kick off with a bang. Known as Arupunte (“At the Bridge”) in Genoese dialect (we are at the farthest edge of Emilia), it is an irresistible village of stone houses in the typical Apennine style, including a great number of fine “tower houses”, a few steps from the emerald waters of the Trebbia. Just below the village lies the beach of the same name, while by following a little path that leaves the village and climbs the right bank of the river for about 15 minutes, you reach the even more pristine “Spiaggia della Valle Inferno”.

It is also one of the best-preserved settlements in the whole valley and deserves a good stroll before setting off along the Via del Cifalco. Its name echoes the one once given to the valley of the Bobbio stream, anciently known as the “Valle Organa”. This matters to us because it suggests that, once on the other bank, a path continued as far as Bobbio, of which no certain traces remain today.

Ponte Organasco is a place steeped in history: from the 13th century it was the seat of a Franciscan settlement guarding the bridge over the Trebbia. Even before then, it housed a monastic cell. It was defended by a castle whose remains are still visible within the fabric of other buildings. The oratory of San Carlo, dating from 1622, is still in good condition, with exposed stonework; but far older is the oratory of Sant’Agostino, just outside the village, which dates back to the 11th century and stood right on the Caminus Januae, which largely followed the floor of the Val Trebbia down to the plain.

Incidentally, over the course of its history, at least five bridges have followed one another here. The one called “Roman”, which collapsed in 1923, was not the first but the second, that is, the one rebuilt after the flood of 1610 that destroyed the original medieval structure (thought to date from the 13th century). In short, people here have never been able to do without a bridge over the Trebbia, on which the village’s importance as a crossroads of many routes probably depended.

Cerignale (708 m a.s.l.) is, in a sense, the “moral” starting point of the walk, as well as the logistical one, since spending the first night here is strongly recommended. With two hotels and as many restaurants, it will seem a metropolis compared with the traces of human presence you will have to make do with over the following days. So give free rein to your sociability with the welcoming locals.

There would be a great deal to say about Cerignale, both historically and in terms of its natural setting, and even more about what it represents today. The village was closely bound up with the fortunes of nearby Cariseto, of which it was nothing more than a satellite (whereas today it is the latter that belongs to the Comune of Cerignale). Rich in spring water and fountains, it lies on a natural terrace surrounded by hazels and Turkey oaks, right at the altitude where the first beeches begin to appear. Beyond the old village, which boasts a great number of characteristic stone houses in an excellent state of preservation, you reach the parish church of San Lorenzo, built in 1540 and already looking towards the confluence of the Trebbia and the Aveto. Anyone strolling through the village will notice the signs of various works that express the commitment of the local administration over recent decades to bringing modernity to the traditional rural landscape of our mountains, which instead tend to empty and die. Whatever one’s electoral preferences, credit must be given to a great many generous attempts to counter the historical, economic and demographic hardship of this kind of territory. Cerignale has thus become a point of reference in the Ligurian Apennines for issues and debates concerning rural development and mountain depopulation, with a rich calendar of events and initiatives well worth following.

After Cerignale you come to Oneto, one of the oldest settlements in the area. It is a placid hamlet, with many fountains and a fine view over the valley. It is mentioned, as Castrum de Oneto, in a diploma of Emperor Otto I of Saxony drawn up in 972 AD. Despite the Latin place name, no trace of the castle can be seen; and yet it is no surprise that there once was one, considering the position of the castle of Cariseto, set more or less in a mirror position on the other side of the ridge. The supposed link between the two fortifications seems all the more plausible in light of the fact that both fiefs were granted by Frederick Barbarossa to Obizzo Malaspina in the same year, 1164. From Oneto begins the climb to Monte delle Tane, the first summit on the Cifalco ridge.

Apart from the summit of M. delle Tane, the first opportunity to leave the ridge comes by descending to Cariseto (982 m a.s.l.). This is a crucial place for grasping the historical implications and the scenic beauty of the Via del Cifalco. Today it appears as a small cluster of houses surrounded by dense woods of beech and Turkey oak, with streams and springs that make it a jewel set in luxuriant nature. On a stern ophiolitic rock overlooking the village stand the fascinating ruins of the Malaspina castle. It is documented in 1052, when it was granted by Emperor Henry III to the monastery of San Paolo di Mezzano, but it may even have risen on the remains of a hillfort built by the Ligures in pre-Roman times. In 1164 Frederick Barbarossa enfeoffed it to Obizzo Malaspina, who escorted him to Tortona along the now famous ride along the Via del Cifalco, passing through Cariseto and thereby saving him from the troops of Pontremoli. In this castle the Malaspina adopted the infamous “Codes of Cariseto”, whose application was later extended to many nearby areas. Even today, in the upper Val Trebbia, people use the expression “Cariseto justice” to refer to a very severe judgement or very harsh penalties, which at the time were rigorously carried out in public.

In 1540 it passed to the Fieschi, who largely took refuge there after the failure of the Fieschi conspiracy of 1547, recounted above. The castle fell into the hands of the Doria, who administered it until the abolition of the Ligurian Imperial Fiefs. From the castle a breathtaking view unfolds over a sea of woods and silence. It is a relatively short detour from the ridge route and therefore absolutely recommended.

Taking instead the path on the opposite side from the one heading to Cariseto, you reach, in a far more substantial amount of time, Ottone Soprano and Ottone. Ottone Soprano (760 m a.s.l.) was rebuilt after the landslides that destroyed the original 11th-century settlements. In the nearby hamlet of Semensi (860 m a.s.l.) there was also a Malaspina tower, of which no trace remains today.

Continuing beyond Ottone Soprano you arrive at Ottone, the municipal seat and the last Comune of Emilia before the border with Liguria. Founded in the 10th century AD and fortified in the 12th century (the castle dates from 1164), it is said that the settlement is in fact even older than that: “U’Tun” is supposedly a word of Celtic origin meaning “brook”, in reference to the Rio Ottone and the Rio Ventra, the two streams that encircle Ottone on either side before plunging into the Trebbia. According to a different interpretation, however, the original name “Otona” is owed to Emperor Otto I of Saxony, who certainly stopped here.

In Ottone the Doria made themselves remembered for their “Statutes”, borrowed from the deadly “Codes of Cariseto” previously spread by the Malaspina on the other side of the Cifalco.

Ottone has always been at the centre of various trade routes: not only the Antica Via del Cifalco (with respect to which Ottone is a detour that forces us to leave the ridge road) and the Caminus Januae, but also many other mule tracks linking it to the paths on the left bank of the Trebbia, towards the marquisate of Campi and the Val Boreca.

Today, to anyone speeding past by car on the Statale, it seems at first sight gloomy and austere. The built-up area in fact reveals a delightful historic village, with a discreet and deep-rooted village life, as well as various “bathing” options in summer, thanks to several access points to the Trebbia and the delightful Botasso waterfalls, where you can cool off. The turn-off for the falls is met on the left along the path descending from Ottone Soprano: an extraordinary succession of pools carved out by the Rio Ottone leading to a waterfall a few metres high, the destination of refreshing summer swims for a still rather select public.

More or less at the same height as Ottone, but on the Aveto side, lies Orezzoli. A popular variant led merchants right through here, as there were several places to eat and rest. This is no longer the case today, neither at Orezzoli on this side nor at Orezzoli on the other side (also known as Connio delle Cascine); indeed, the variant has also lost much of its scenic interest, since an asphalt road now cuts across the forest halfway up the slope to link these two hamlets first with the “Bivio Veri” and then with Cerignale.

Few other attractions seem to justify a descent to Orezzoli today, which can just be glimpsed on the left, from above, from the Via del Cifalco after passing the “Bivio Veri”, on the way to M. Dego.

A pity, because the place has considerable historical importance. It was precisely from the first marquis of Orezzoli, Corrado Malaspina “the Elder”, that in 1221 the split into the two famous branches originated, reflected in their respective coats of arms: he was the founder of the “dry thorn” branch, which controlled all the family’s territories west of the river Magra, while his cousin Obizzo Malaspina founded the “flowering thorn” branch and turned his sphere of influence towards the territories east of the same river. Moreover, Corrado the Elder himself married the daughter of Emperor Frederick II, after saving her life during a hunt in the woods of Orezzoli.

But that is not all: it was once again at Orezzoli, so it seems, that the famous Malaspina Statutes were drawn up, with the dreadful Laws (or Codes) of Cariseto, later borrowed by the Fieschi and the Doria. Of all this, no trace remains at Orezzoli, and both hamlets are almost completely uninhabited. The most observant will notice, at Orezzoli on the other side, a hut that recalls the so-called “barchi”, ancient Celtic buildings used to store straw and hay. It is precisely the hope of bringing life and light back to forgotten places like Orezzoli that drives the (re)launch of the Antica Via del Cifalco.

Before reaching the summit of M. Dego, you meet the turn-off for Toveraia, a hamlet of very ancient origins, since San Gaudenzio di Toveraia is mentioned in a document signed by Emperor Otto I of Saxony in 962 AD. Of all this, sadly, only evocations remain today, along with a small group of mostly uninhabited houses, grass climbing over the stones and a film of dust over the memory of the place that once was.

With the summit of M. Dego begins the sequence of the most spectacular peaks of the walk. On top of this mountain, since time immemorial, a feast has been held every year in honour of the church dedicated to Our Lady of Lourdes, which was built by the veterans of the 1915-1918 war from this area to thank her for their return home. The tradition is still alive today and still draws a great number of devotees from the neighbouring valleys and from many other, even remote, corners of the province of Genoa.

This stretch of the Apennines has always been much frequented: traces have been found here of an “ospitale” run by monks, who provided charity and assistance to travellers. The summit meadows were a classic camping place for the muleteers travelling the Via del Cifalco, especially in summer. Since mules graze at night too, this also made it possible to save on the cost of fodder. The men slept in the shade of the beeches or under makeshift shelters built with the mules’ pack-saddles or with oilcloths brought up from the valley (called “patìgge”). Now that the mules are gone, it is more often families of wild boar or packs of wolves that can be seen roaming these clearings nowadays.

M. Oramara (1522 m a.s.l.) is the highest point of the Via del Cifalco, which passes just below it. Old maps probably record it under the name “Scorteghero”. When the name changed is uncertain, but it is reasonable to think that the present place name refers to some episode of local history whose protagonist was some unfortunate soul who met a nasty end right there.

Past the Rifugio Prati di Foppiano, the ridge continues with Montarlone (1500 m a.s.l.), the result of the progressive contraction of Monte Lupo (“Wolf Mountain”), or Montarlù to the valley folk. The historical name says everything about its main visitors.

Anecdotes and legends

Fontana del Figliolo

A medieval anecdote of uncertain date explains the origins of the place name. A newborn baby from the marquisate of Casanova had to be carried for baptism to Alpepiana, on the Aveto side, since only there was there a baptismal font (for this reason it must have happened before 1076, the year in which a baptismal font is known for certain to have existed at Rovegno). It was winter and the weather conditions were extreme. The party, exhausted and sure that the child would not reach Alpepiana alive, baptised him in that fountain at the foot of Montarlone, on the Trebbia side, which from that day bears his name (“the Fountain of the Little Son”).

Given that it is advisable to tackle the summit of Montarlone further on, just before Passo Vallersone, by means of a specially signposted path (see the “Walking the trail” section), the turn-off to the right immediately after the Rifugio Foppiano would lead to the Fontana del Figliolo (though it is not signposted).

Continuing instead on the left and then straight on through the ridge beechwood, just past the turn-off for the summit of Montarlone you reach Passo Vallersone, from which the road to Casanova descends on the right.

This detour is a real spectacle, perhaps one of the most memorable stretches, in natural terms, of the Trebbia-Aveto ridge. Just below the pass begins a profusion of springs, sources, pools and fountains, in an arcadia of wild yet pleasant nature. In summer there are various options for a refreshing dip in the icy waters of these brooks and rivulets, among tadpoles, frogs and big dragonflies. Suddenly the landscape changes abruptly: the beechwoods give way to semi-arid areas and you begin walking on very dark, extremely crumbly clay-schist rocks, on which helichrysum and other Mediterranean plants grow (the locals call these rises “M. Nero”), before returning to the dense woods.

At a certain point in the descent, a little below the sources of the Pescia stream, you come across the “Fontana del Vino”. It was so called because it stood in a placid clearing where the muleteers refreshed themselves before resuming their journey. Some maintain that the name is in truth owed to a particular group of muleteers, namely those who carried wine towards the Val d’Aveto in goatskin flasks, especially between the 16th and 17th centuries. According to village gossip, they would therefore allow themselves the odd small clandestine “withdrawal” from the goods they carried when they found themselves together near this spring. Which also lightened the load, and the soul, before the stern climb towards Passo Vallersone, which took them back to the Strada del Cifalco.

Seen like this, with a few houses that are indeed “new” (or at any rate few that look old), Casanova may at first sight arouse a certain indifference. And yet the place name probably derives from the fact that members of the Mulazzo branch of the Malaspina family, later called “di Casanova”, settled here “ex novo”. It is established that right here the Malaspina had a castle, now vanished. The fief then passed to the Doria in 1656, until the abolition of the Ligurian Imperial Fiefs.

It was also at Casanova that the banditry of the Cifalco found a moment of partial pacification in 1571. That year, in fact, a great number of people banished by the Republic of Genoa and from the fiefs assigned to the Doria gathered here. They were all granted amnesty, and the ceremony ended with the peacemaking rite of drinking from the same bowl by the representatives of the various families or kinship groups (see Pace di Casanova, A.S.Ge., Atti del Senato, filza 1455, doc. n. 41). Note that, until the beginning of the 20th century, Casanova had over 1000 residents; anyone visiting today will wonder where they all went.

A short walk links Casanova to the medieval bridge of Canfernasca over the Pescia stream, a symbol of the territory of the Comune of Rovegno together with the adjacent Mulino del Principe, which already appears in a notarial deed of 1491, built on the remains of a Malaspina castle. The arched shape of the bridge is picture-postcard perfect, and the view alone is worth a detour of many kilometres to admire it.

Further on, crossing the “Strada di Chiavari”, you reach Fontanigorda in less than half an hour (NB: the village can also be reached from above, via the road that descends from Passo del Gifarco). It is a small comune of 284 inhabitants in the upper Val Trebbia. The first trace of the place name appears in a notarial deed of 1182, which refers to the locality “super fontem in gorda”. This was in all likelihood the spring of the Rio Cugno, which flowed “in gorda”, that is, into artificial basins created for breeding fish. It is an activity particularly suited to the very “watery” area between Fontanigorda and Casanova; it is therefore no surprise that it has not been entirely lost, given the presence even today of river aquariums devoted to the practice of aquaculture. Today Fontanigorda has undoubtedly lost much of its vitality, but a few key shops hold out, along with a close-knit community of residents and holidaymakers. It is also one of those villages where in summer you still see children playing in the churchyard and along the cool caruggi of the village. In the age of generational brain-rot brought to you by smart-phone and tablet, that is no small thing.

These surroundings are also notable because at Loco (on the valley floor, a little below Fontanigorda, in the Comune of Rovegno: a place too far from the Cifalco to recommend reaching it on foot) lived for two years Giorgio Caproni, one of the greatest Italian poets of the twentieth century, who worked there as a primary school teacher. His poetics of memory, of neglected and derelict places, is ideal reading for this journey. He dedicated no fewer than eight poems to the Val Trebbia: “Ballo a Fontanigorda”, “Da una lettera di Rina”, “Nebbia”, “Lasciando Loco”, “Ottone”, “Di un luogo preciso descritto per enumerazione”, “Statale 45” and “Così lontano l’azzurro tenebra della tua Trebbia dove ora vivi”.

Incidentally, Ernest Hemingway’s supposed visit to the Trebbia and Aveto area has never been established, contrary to what is all too often claimed, particularly by those who have wanted to exploit the idea for commercial purposes.

Resuming the Strada del Cifalco from Passo Vallersone, it crosses the Passi di Ertola and then Esola, ancient junctions for those who had to leave the ridge to descend to Genoa via Passo della Scoffera and the Val Bisagno. Before the fork leading to the summit of M. Roccabruna there is a clearing at 1361 m a.s.l. It was, and still is today, known as “u fò sparpagiò”, that is, “the sprawling beech”, with its twisted, intertwined branches. The place name, undoubtedly informal, seems to indicate a spot very exposed to the winds, since the beechwood stopped there. Here invisible spring waters well up, and it was a stopping place for caravans, as well as a lookout over the crest as far as M. Caucaso.

Following the ridge, you reach M. Roccabruna (1418 m a.s.l.), which marks one of its most panoramic points. From its summit, which owes its name to the dark colour of the ophiolitic serpentine rock it is made of, you can visually command much of the Val Trebbia and a broad stretch of the Val d'Aveto.

A little beyond the fork for the summit of M. Roccabruna, here we are at the one for M. Gifarco (1380 m a.s.l.), perhaps the most eagerly awaited mountain, since it is the one that gives its name to the whole walk.

Anecdotes and legends

Below Monte Gifarco, 1944

Some crossings of the Cifalco have taken on dramatic tones. During the round-ups of 1944, about 1000 soldiers of the German Wehrmacht set out from the Val Fontanabuona and, after routing the partisans on M. Caucaso, continued their march along the Strada del Cifalco. On reaching the Valico del Fregarolo, they turned off towards Casoni to order the parish priest, on pain of execution by firing squad, to hand over the list of names of some young men of the area who had evaded conscription. He somehow managed to convince them that they were missing or dead. The soldiers calmed down and continued their march, leaving the village intact (Barbagelata had been burned in similar circumstances shortly before). By a cruel twist of fate, right below M. Gifarco a patrol of partisans inadvertently came under enemy fire. Two of them fell, while others managed to escape. They were found the next day by a group of people that included the late Guido Ferretti, an authoritative local historian and great connoisseur of the area, to whose work we owe this and other stories as well as many of the historical insights on this site. It was he who noted how, by the irony of fate, the two young partisans died at the hands of the Germans beside the only summit on the ridge that bears a name probably of Germanic origin.

Expectations will not be disappointed. The final assault on the top, though short, is great fun: you have to squeeze into a rock passage perhaps built for the purpose by prehistoric peoples. Indeed, some ruins found right here would seem to prove that M. Gifarco was once a lookout post that allowed customs officers, in the feudal era, to watch over a long stretch of the road, as perhaps also on nearby M. Castello del Fante.

Perhaps it is the intimidating appearance of this ophiolitic rock, which seems to have burst through the beechwood from the bowels of the earth, that has made it so frequented since ancient times. However, its location also makes it more interesting strategically, particularly compared with M. Roccabruna, which is higher but in a less defensible position.

On the summit of M. Gifarco you will also find a surprise: an iconic sword in the stone is driven into it. All very evocative, but allow us a few clarifications. It is certainly a landmark for the many hikers who reach this summit, so much so that many were saddened when, in July 2024, it was discovered that someone had stolen it; an episode that, moreover, followed various other acts of vandalism committed in previous years. However, not only is the placing of the sword on the summit of the Gifarco a very recent affair (until about 30 years ago it stood in the “Bosco delle Fate”, above Fontanigorda); its very creation, with a dedication to San Galgano, looks like a contrived operation. Galgano was in fact a 12th-century Tuscan knight who is not known ever to have passed through these parts: the original sword in the stone of the knight Galgano is kept in the Eremo di Montesiepi at Chiusdino, in Tuscany. In short, all well and good if the image of the sword in the stone feeds the imagination of enthusiasts (above all children, happy to see that a replica of it was planted again on top of the Gifarco after 2024), but all that glitters is not gold. Our mountains are already extremely rich in history, culture and traditions of their own; there is no need to go looking elsewhere for spurious narratives in order to bring the charm of these lands fully to life.

Leaving the summit of the Gifarco behind, you reach the pass of the same name. Here you meet, on the right, the mule track descending to Fontanigorda, while on the left it leads down to Brignole. For those with the time and the courage to go there (the climb back up will be stiff), it will prove a little treasure chest of secrets. The village appears suddenly out of the woods and consists of a fine succession of stone houses, among brooks gushing along the sides of the paved lanes. An atmosphere of old, silent rural civilisation pervades the little village’s main street, all the way to the Chiesa di Santa Maria Maggiore. The family of the same name also originates from this small hamlet: one of the most important merchant dynasties of Liguria, known since the 13th century. A few hundred metres from the village, walkers also have various options for a swim in the Aveto.

Continuing instead along the ridge after Passo Gifarco, you leave on the right the (barely visible) turn-off for M. Castello del Fante (1390 m), which was perhaps known in ancient times as the pasture of the Erba Bella, since it was the only summit of the ridge topped by sizeable meadows.

Anecdotes and legends

From Casoni to Orezzoli, summer 1924

The Via del Cifalco has been the scene of epic adventures even in relatively recent times, and many of them are joyful. It is said, for example, that one evening in the summer of 1924 three young men from Casoni di Fontanigorda (u Gioxepìn du Ferretti, u Stinèttu du Pierìn e u Giuvanìn di Drìe) decided to walk all the way to Orezzoli to meet the Genoese accordion player known as “U Segùndu”, whom they wanted to engage for their own patron saint’s feast as well. The road from Casoni to Orezzoli is long! It would appear (which sounds very optimistic) that thanks to their brisk pace they reached their destination in only three hours of walking (in our view, it would take at least five). So they arrived without trouble and enjoyed the evening with their peers, amid dancing and merriment. When it was time to go back, the three hesitated about staying the night, encouraged by the invitations of the villagers of Orezzoli; however, not having told their families they would be out, they preferred to head home.

Unfortunately, their paraffin lamp was no longer enough to guide them in the dead of night, especially once they reached the stretch between M. Oramara and Montarlone. Clouds hid the moon, and uncertainty about which way to go took hold of them at certain key junctions. And yet they managed to pull together, relying on their intuition and experience, and arrived safe and sound in Casoni at first light, with U Segùndu’s promise to liven up the next village feast in their pocket!

At the Valico del Fregarolo, the Antica Via del Cifalco crosses the “strada ronea”, or “Strada di Chiavari”, coming from the Val d’Aveto and heading on to Casoni di Fontanigorda and then to Fontanigorda. Here we are at a crossroads teeming with anecdotes and legends, largely linked to the passage of smugglers. Indeed, just as with the later Passo della Rocca, in the 17th century Prince Doria forbade transit through the pass in order to ensure that duty was paid at the toll house of Torriglia. It is therefore reasonable to think that those who kept on passing this way had something to hide; by doing so, they evaded the tolls imposed by the Prince’s Camera Eccellentissima.

The first point of interest after the pass is without doubt the Lago della Nave, at 1173 m a.s.l. Here we are right in the middle of a Site of Community Importance (SIC; see the “Nature and landscape, from the mountains to the sea” section), and biodiversity finds a secret refuge here. It is a curious hollow that freezes in winter and gives rise to a boundless proliferation of tadpoles in May. It was also an important stop for the muleteers, because it served to water the mules at one of the few bodies of water lying directly on the route.

After the little chapel of Cardenosa comes that of Costafinale, reduced to a heap of rubble. In fact, the hamlet of Costafinale (1111 m a.s.l.) occupies a commanding position over the Val Trebbia; it is therefore no coincidence that, from the time of the Lombards, the spur descending from the village to the valley marked the border between the territory of the Abbey of Patrania and that of the Corte di Alpepiana. Its very name (from the Latin “finis”) once again indicates the frontier character of many of these areas. Between the two chapels, that of Cardenosa and that of Costafinale, near Monte Pietrabianca, if you turn to the left you see the sea for the first time.

Barbagelata (1115 m a.s.l.), Barbaseà in the local dialect, is the landing point of the Trebbia-Aveto ridge, after which the caravans descended, or before which they climbed, along different mule tracks depending on the coastal place they were heading for or coming from.

Anecdotes and legends

Barbagelata and the bandit Billo

In reality, it was not only merchants and travellers who benefited from Barbagelata’s frontier character: it was in fact the place where, in the 16th century, the bandit Stefano Cordano, known as “Billo”, ran riot. It appears that in 1584, after he had been arrested, probably in the Podesteria of Roccatagliata (to which Barbagelata belonged), by members of the Biggio kinship group from the marquisate of Santo Stefano d’Aveto, it was they who found themselves put on trial. The prosecution claimed that they had violated the borders of the Most Serene Republic of Genoa; and in the end it was the Biggio themselves who were ordered to compensate the bandit Billo for the harm he had suffered!

The suggestions concerning the ancient settlement of a northern people, to whom the place name is supposedly owed, were already mentioned above, in the “Historical notes on the territory” section. It cannot be ruled out, however, that the name is simply due instead to the often inclement weather. The village in fact lies at the end of a ridge that enjoys no protection whatsoever from the elements. It was also the place where, wherever they came from, the caravans stopped for the night. From the 13th century there was also a monastic settlement set up to assist travellers.

Barbagelata was burned by the Germans during the Second World War, which explains why fewer historic buildings remain than we might expect. Perhaps this is also why it appears to travellers as quiet and perhaps even lifeless.

A little beyond Barbagelata, a short up-and-down leads to Passo della Scoglina, where the climb towards M. Caucaso begins. Along this stretch of the walk you come across a very striking case of “river capture”. The Rio dell'Acquapendente has eroded the fragile clay-schist layers of the ridge, pushing back the watershed and "capturing" part of the headwater branches that once fed or belonged to the upper course of the Aveto, which rises near M. Caucaso. This is the “capture of the Aveto”: this stream then runs for a few hundred metres within the basin of the Malvaro stream, which descends south of the watershed and flows into the Lavagna. What has not (yet?) been captured of the Aveto remains separated from the waters of the Malvaro by a thin little rocky crest. Thanks to this precarious obstacle, the Aveto hangs in the balance for a few kilometres, until its flow increases through the inflow of the Gramizza and Rezzoaglio streams, tipping it decisively to the north of the watershed. For a matter of centimetres, its waters, instead of reaching the Tigullio in a few kilometres via the Lavagna, must travel thousands before flowing into the Adriatic, after joining the Trebbia and then the Po.

The “maritime” Apennines

As already explained at length above (see the “Nature and landscape, from the mountains to the sea” section), M. Caucaso divides the part of the “continental” Apennines that looks towards the mountains and descends towards the plain from the part that instead plunges rather abruptly towards the Mediterranean.

The route follows this watershed for a few kilometres, in the descent from the summit of M. Caucaso westwards, almost as far as the Passo di Pietra Cavallina. This rock (a peculiar sandstone formation about two metres high and relatively isolated in the surrounding landscape) can only be reached by means of a detour, since at the pass the path turns decisively left towards Neirone.

You pass through Faggio Rotondo (“Round Beech”), a placid spot where a centuries-old beech really does exist, near a ruined house. This area of Faggio Rotondo was an important checkpoint and refuge for the partisans of the famous Divisione Cichero, who operated among the mountains of the Ligurian hinterland. At the site there is a commemorative plaque dedicated to the crew of a bomber lost on 12 October 1944 while attempting to drop supplies of weapons and food to the local partisans. Of the various aircraft shot down by the Nazi-Fascist forces, it was the only one never to be found.

Passing Faggio Rotondo and Pian del Pero to reach the Comune of Neirone, and then down the little valley of the same name to Gattorna, you magically find yourself in the catchment area of the Val Fontanabuona.

Reserved and all too often underrated, it is a valley very different from those enjoyed so far, and it certainly deserves a discussion of its own. Even its name (a rare case in Italy) does not coincide with that of the watercourse running through it, the Lavagna stream, which manages to change its name to Entella after receiving its tributaries the Sturla and the Graveglia, just a few kilometres before… reaching its mouth, right by the town of Lavagna.

Speaking of the qualities of the Lavagna stream, it is said to be (according to the most widely accepted interpretation) the “fiumana bella” (“fair river”) which the Supreme Poet, Dante Alighieri, places “intra Siestri e Chiaveri” (“between Siestri and Chiaveri”) in Canto XIX of Purgatorio (lines 100-102). For a long time scholars believed that “Siestri” was in fact Sestri Levante, but this would lead to various geographical inconsistencies, since between Sestri Levante and Chiavari, apart from the Gromolo valley, there are very few “rivers”, fair or foul as they may be. Moreover, it is established that Dante passed through the Val Fontanabuona: according to some, this happened on the occasion of a controversial journey to Paris; according to others in 1306, coming from Verona and heading for Lunigiana; or again some time later, on his way to Milan to meet Emperor Arrigo (Henry) VII, in 1311.

Slate is not the only excellence that has made its way in the Val Fontanabuona over the centuries (see the “Rural civilisation on the Salt Roads” section). At Lorsica, the Comune that also includes the hamlet of Barbagelata, traces still survive, though very hidden, of an age-old tradition of damask weaving, documented from the 16th century as widespread throughout the valley and today told in the Damask Museum.

But every village has its own peculiarities and its own stories to tell: at the locality of Castello, a small village in the Comune of Favale di Malvaro, which the Via del Cifalco does not pass through but which can be glimpsed during the ascent of M. Caucaso, a small Waldensian cemetery recalls the sufferings inflicted on the local Protestants at the time of the wars of religion.

Anecdotes and legends

The priest of Roccatagliata and the potatoes

Besides being very beautiful and brimming with history and architecture, Roccatagliata was the setting for an episode of enormous social significance, told at the International Potato Museum at Villa Rocca (off the Cifalco route, being on the opposite bank of the Aveto). In the 17th century, when the potato was imported from the Americas and its enormous potential for Europe’s food security was immediately recognised, it was not easy to persuade rural populations to introduce its cultivation on a large scale. Frightened by superstitions and by the poisonous fruits (in the potato, only the tuber is edible), they refused to adapt to the change more or less all over our continent. While in Russia and Prussia the revolts were put down in blood, in our parts this was not necessary. One Sunday, in a year that is not known, the priest of Roccatagliata, at the end of Mass, went with his parishioners onto the parvis of the village’s beautiful church, built by Cardinal Luca Fieschi in 1328. He declared that God would protect everyone from all harm and, theatrically, began eating potatoes in front of an astonished crowd. The word of mouth that followed, from village to village across the valleys and passes, soon led to mass acceptance of the new food. It thus entered the diet of the inhabitants of all Liguria and, by extension, of all Italy, helping to save many from the hunger and hardship to which they would otherwise have been condemned in the centuries to come.

Before descending towards the valley floor, the hamlet of Roccatagliata is worth a detour from Neirone. It is an 11th-century medieval village built, probably, on even earlier Lombard foundations.

Resuming the route from Neirone, for the time being we recommend taking the asphalt road that reaches Gattorna in about five kilometres; and this despite the existence of a splendid woodland path along the turbulent Neirone stream, part of the Itinerario dei Feudi Fliscani (IFF), which can be picked up right by the main square of Neirone. Neglect and decay have slowly taken hold of this stretch of path, which otherwise holds great potential. We are supporting the restoration of the path’s walkability; it is currently passable again, although its complete rehabilitation will unfortunately take years. It is not just a matter of fallen trees and landslides. The gorge of the Beo Grande, a brook that flows into the Neirone, we jokingly call the “Valley of wonders”: rubbish bags, household appliances, plastics and microplastics and other waste material invite the walker to a serious (and stern) reflection on the relationship between humankind and nature and on the system of values needed to preserve our planet from degradation.

Once on the valley floor, you enter little Gattorna, heralded from afar by the imposing Santuario di Nostra Signora della Guardia looming over the village. Gattorna is a simple little village on the Lavagna stream, one of those crossed by a Statale road, where you do not lack things like a video game museum or shoe shops called “Scarpe Diem”. It nevertheless remains a peaceful place and a strategic stop before venturing up the climb along the right flank of the Val Fontanabuona.

After crossing the little wooden bridge over the Lavagna and, shortly afterwards, the far more interesting 16th-century stone bridge over the Rio Rosso, the road climbs towards Cassanesi, a pleasant village that already has an eastern Ligurian flavour.

The path climbs until it meets the Itinerario Storico Colombiano and touches Passo dei Casetti, where it rejoins the Via del Sale/Via del Mare (formerly known as the Via dell’Antola). From here we enter a landscape of an entirely maritime character, which accompanies us along a route known as the “sentiero dei due golfi” (“path of the two gulfs”), since it looks out on the left over the Tigullio and on the right over the Golfo Paradiso.

On the slopes of M. Orsena, a lane branches off to the right leading to the summit, where the Santuario Nostra di Caravaggio (615 m a.s.l.) stands. A focal point of devotion for the inhabitants of Santa Maria del Campo (a hamlet of Rapallo), who brought a small painting of the Madonna here in the 17th century, it soon became a destination of pilgrimages. For a long time it therefore suffered the jealousy of the far more renowned and powerful Santuario di Montallegro, which limited its popularity.

And yet it certainly deserves a visit, if only for the spectacular view over the whole Tigullio as far as Genoa, which unfolds beyond the holm-oak wood and the clearings of crocuses and primroses surrounding the sanctuary at the end of winter. On the other side, along the ridge that reaches the Manico del Lume and encircles the Tigullio as far as Chiavari, heather tinges the slope when it flowers in September/October.

The site is also notable for a geological curiosity: on the limestone slabs of the stairway leading to the sanctuary, fossil traces of “helminthoids” have been found, ancient organisms that lived over 50 million years ago, when these mountains were nothing but the floor of a great ocean. Their presence expresses once again the inextricable union of sea and mountain that can be felt everywhere in the Ligurian Levante.

At a certain point, paths are signposted descending to Recco and, a little further on, to Camogli. Inhabited since the Bronze and Iron Ages, according to legend its place name derives from “Ca’ delle mogli” (“House of the wives”), who, the story goes, waited long for their men to return from the sea, while the men in turn could make out their homes from afar by their brightly coloured façades. Today it is, together with Portofino, the most renowned seaside resort of the Ligurian Levante, with a fantastic little harbour, the iconic Castello della Dragonara and a fine beach. Those who have time to go down and climb back up (perhaps staying a night) should not miss the chance to spend some time there.

This long crossing of the mountains between the Val Fontanabuona and the Tigullio along the “sentiero dei due golfi” ends at Ruta, set on the pass beyond which open the gates of the Parco del M. di Portofino. To be precise, the path arrives near the Romanesque church of Ruta, known as the “Millenaria”, about ten minutes’ walk from the village. It stands at the crossroads of the so-called Strada di Bana, on a route that is probably prehistoric, also used in Roman times and right up to the end of the 19th century. Leaving aside the numerous restorations and alterations, including the fire set by Napoleon Bonaparte’s French troops under the command of General Massena, the original core probably dates back to the 7th-8th century, in the heart of the Lombard period. It was precisely during this period that the cult of Saint Michael, “enemy of Satan”, to whom the Chiesa Millenaria is dedicated, spread throughout Europe.

The Parco del M. di Portofino: arriving at Portofino Mare and the end of the Via del Cifalco

From Ruta and its viewpoint along the Via Aurelia, a stairway begins. At its start, the path that will lead us to Portofino Mare through the territory of the Parco del M. di Portofino is signposted for the first time.

This paved crêuza, which first climbs and then runs level along the Sella della Gaixella, within the wonderful natural and scenic setting of the park, offers us a network of paths that would take years to get to know thoroughly. Among the many places reachable via one of the detours, we cannot fail to mention at least a few.

World-famous is San Fruttuoso, reachable only on foot or by boat and recognisable by its marvellous abbey. According to tradition, the relics of San Fruttuoso, bishop of Tarragona, where he was martyred during the Roman persecutions in 259 AD, were kept in loco until 711 AD. At the time of the first Arab invasion of Spain, Bishop Prosperus and his followers decided to take them to safety elsewhere in the Mediterranean. They thus ended up at Capodimonte, where there almost certainly already existed a monastery erected by the Benedictine monks of the Order of San Colombano of Bobbio. Thanks to substantial donations, including that of the Lombard Empress Adelaide, from the 11th century the monastery found itself administering vast territories in every corner of the Tigullio, but also further east along the Ligurian Levante and further north, along the Apennine ridge almost as far as the river Po.

Anecdotes and legends

San Fruttuoso and the wreck of the Croesus

Inside the abbey there is also the crypt with the tombs of the Doria, which also houses those of two sisters connected with an anecdote that still stirs the imagination of San Fruttuoso’s visitors. On 24 April 1855 the British steamship Croesus was sailing from Genoa to the Crimea. When it came level with the bay of San Fruttuoso, a fire broke out. Panic soon seized the sailors. The vessel had no choice but to head desperately for land. The inhabitants of the village, at the time mostly fishermen, generously threw themselves into the rough sea with their boats. The desperation of the castaways, clinging to them convulsively, overturned the boat of the Avegno sisters. Caterina reached safety, while Maria drowned along with 24 of the 300 soldiers. The sea gave back the 25 bodies only five days later, by which time the last fragments of the steamship had only just finished burning.

The Doria ended up descending on San Fruttuoso too: in 1125 Martino Doria had the church of San Matteo built in Genoa, subject to the Abbey of San Fruttuoso; from then on a partnership was established that lasted for centuries, which also gave rise to the Torre Doria, commissioned by Andrea Doria himself in 1562, which still dominates the village today.

After a long decline, the church ended up being downgraded to a parish in 1885. Today the abbey is the property of the Fondo Ambiente Italiano (FAI), which has contributed to a very well executed restoration. It can be visited.

Note that the beach, lovely though besieged in high season, did not exist until 1915, the year in which a flood, along with a great deal of damage, left it to us as a legacy.

It hardly needs recalling that, in 1954, the statue of the “Christ of the Abyss” was placed on the seabed of the bay, to the delight of thousands of tourists who seem to find the thing particularly exciting. On this point, the considerations expressed about the sword in the stone on M. Gifarco apply mutatis mutandis, with the aggravating factor that this Christ fuels a mass hyper-tourism which, on M. Gifarco, people at least still manage to do without.

Another good alternative for concluding the Antica Via del Cifalco is the descent to Santa Margherita Ligure. “Santa” is a renowned seaside resort with a long tradition of holidaymaking behind it, a little (but only a little) less luxurious and elitist than Portofino, but also more relaxed and holiday-like.

From the historic core of Corte (the part of the town that runs from the harbour pier to the castle), the town has grown considerably, driven by foreign and Genoese families who, since the end of the 12th century, have chosen it as their summer residence. Its present shape, which tends to spread up to the slopes of the surrounding mountains, was instead determined by the haemorrhage of concrete that exploded after the Second World War. Still, compared with neighbouring Rapallo, it got off lightly.

And yet “Santa” remains a place with a most pleasant atmosphere and also a discreet and often hidden everyday village life, with various ways down to the sea (free and equipped beaches), especially along the stretch towards Portofino.

Among the various points of interest, the unmissable Villa Durazzo stands out. On the hill overlooking Corte stood an ancient fortress which, in the 16th century, the Durazzo-Pallavicino family had transformed into an elegant Renaissance villa, surrounded by a large park with a view of the sea. An avenue of palms links the villa to the church of San Giacomo. On the balustrade of the garden, adorned with fountains and neat flowerbeds, a row of statues of Greek deities stands out. The presence of this residence and its park lends taste and charm to the whole town and reconciles land and sea in the visitor’s eyes. Access to the garden is public, and the villa can be visited during events (and weddings!).

Santa Margherita is also notable as the birthplace of Camillo Sbarbaro, one of the most important Italian poets of the 1900s. He was the bard of a Liguria much closer to that of the hinterland we have walked through as far as Ruta, a harsh and rugged land, with twisted olive trees and dry-stone walls. His landscapes also reflect his existential condition. Reading Camillo Sbarbaro is perfect for setting out on the Strada del Cifalco.

As explained in the “Planning the journey: stages, detours and maps” section, you can reach Santa Margherita Ligure either by cutting straight across from the Sella della Gaixella, thus passing through Nozarego, or by following the lovely promenade linking Portofino Mare to Paraggi (recently, absurdly, renamed the “Passeggiata dei baci”, the “Promenade of Kisses”: who the devil came up with that idea?) and then continuing along the seafront to Santa Margherita. If you arrive along the seafront, you cannot fail to notice the famous bay of Paraggi, one of the few natural sandy beaches of the Ligurian Levante, in a wooded setting with emerald-coloured water. This remains true, even though Paraggi is threatened by the omnipresence of luxury brands (all belonging, as it happens, to a single group) which, with the connivance of the Italian State, have done everything to strip the soul from this once magical corner, largely succeeding. Continuing towards Santa Margherita, still along the seafront, you will glimpse on the left the Abbazia della Cervara, built by the Benedictines from 1361 onwards. The place name derives from the Latin “sylvaria”, proof that even then it was surrounded by dense tree cover. Today it can be visited: the interior has been fitted out and furnished with lavish means, but in a style that seems intended to chase the tastes of the Serie A footballers who hold parties and weddings there; the terrace, on the other hand, with its garden and centuries-old wisteria, is one of the most spectacular in the whole Mediterranean. The Cervara is, moreover, one piece of a wider network of old religious buildings present in the Parco di Portofino since ancient times: the Eremo di S. Antonio di Niasca (known since 1318), the Chiesa di San Nicolò di Capodimonte (12th century), as well as the Abbazia di S. Fruttuoso di Capodimonte and the “Millenaria” of Ruta already mentioned.

Now that we have digressed, it is time to return to the main mule track, because the detours worth mentioning are over and we are about to chase the last slopes of the Monte, which will finally lead us to Portofino Mare, the end point of our walk.

On the last stretches of the route, when the Sella della Gaixella passes Pietre Strette and begins to descend along the last crêuze cut between the houses of the little hamlets above Portofino, something around us changes all at once.

The evolution of the landscape, however sudden at times, had always been silent, from the beechwoods of the “continental” Apennines to the more varied environment of the Val Fontanabuona, right up to the luxuriant mesophilous woodland of the Parco del M. di Portofino. All of a sudden, this transformation becomes noisier.

Exquisitely elegant villas suddenly appear, with breathtaking views. Clouds of pittosporum (in early May) and jasmine (in June) twine around luxurious stone columns. Olive groves that look sculpted thrive on terraces built by our ancestors, in an extraordinary state of upkeep compared with what we saw in the Val Fontanabuona. The sky vies with the blue of the sea and stands out above vegetable gardens and gardens spectacular for their position and lushness.

But this wave of beauty does not reach the eyes of those who contemplate it on its own. The walkers you meet in the last half hour of the walk, more numerous than all those encountered over the previous days put together, no longer greet you when your eyes meet. Gardeners and other handymen, invariably in uniform, maniacally tend the entrance drives and their English lawns, which look spurious against the canons of the Mediterranean setting in which they were laid out. Meanwhile, old goods lifts are left to rust on the slopes: today quad bikes are more convenient, and indeed they can be heard roaring along the crêuze between San Sebastiano, the Mulino del Gassetta and Olmi. Someone even wanted their own private tennis court, where middle-aged men exclaim in a Lombard accent “focca la bindella!” every time the net stops the ball from reaching the other side of the court by a matter of millimetres.

And yet a timeless enchantment envelops the traveller on finally reaching Portofino Mare. The village’s fortune as a tourist destination in fact began “only” in 1870, when the British consul in Genoa, Yeats Brown, bought the castle of San Giorgio (now “Castello Brown”). From then on came a succession of wealthy families of aristocrats and industrialists, above all British and German (such as the Von Mumms, of Champagne fame), until it became an icon of beauty for the whole world, including (alas) for the people who colonise it when they step off their yachts to head for one of the various high-fashion boutiques in the village.

Yet, elbowing their way among ladies from the Persian Gulf occupying every corner to take “selfies”, pinnacles covered in cypresses soar from the promontory between the two seas, with the little church of San Giorgio and Castello Brown itself wedged among them. How many other sights sum up so perfectly the iconography of the Italian-style Mediterranean landscape? Even in high season, at least on weekdays, the tourists cannot drown out the lapping of the little rowing boats, guardians of the after-all drowsy atmosphere of the Piazzetta.

Of course, for those arriving after several days’ march along the Via del Cifalco, the change is considerable. Not being greeted on the mule tracks above Portofino is a happy memory: here people do not even apologise when they bump into a passer-by. From discreet guests of the mountains, we suddenly find ourselves lost in a crowd in which, dressed as walkers, we feel even more out of place.

Should we then resist this change of register? Probably not. The Via del Cifalco itself, with its silences, its mysteries and the dignity of people who resist the slow but relentless encroachment of Oblivion, reminds us that in every fold of beauty (and of the less beautiful) there are nuances to grasp and ideas to stage in a theatre of the imagination without walls.

Let us accept, then, that the elusive poetry of the Cifalco dissolves just as suddenly as it enveloped us; let us abandon ourselves to this new parade of irresistible, sparkling beauty; let us plunge headlong into this bustle of life and possible joy; let us disguise ourselves too, in linen shirts, boat shoes and little evening dresses; but let us hide, so that our poetic (and critical) gaze may go on following the thread of its thoughts in silence, undisturbed. If, as Goethe said, mountains are silent masters who make silent disciples, then after completing the Via del Cifalco we may consider ourselves trained.
